title: How to find and fix your AEO keywords gap
content:
To improve visibility in AI answer engines, content and SEO marketers need to add AEO keywords gap analysis to their strategies. Traditional SEO keyword gaps show which terms a company isn’t ranking for versus the competition. An AEO keywords gap uses the same principle but with broader criteria, identifying the prompts and questions where a given brand is cited in AI search, but another isn’t.
This guide offers a practical pathway to find and close the AEO keywords gap, identifying AI citation opportunities a company is missing. It covers how to audit current content and competitor coverage, how to spot high-value gaps to close first, how to turn gaps into answer-ready content that gets cited, and how to track whether it’s working.
An AEO keywords gap is the difference between the questions or topics AI answer engines surface versus the questions a brand answers clearly enough to be cited. The gap refers to keywords, topics, questions, and prompts that a brand hasn’t answered clearly enough to be cited in engines like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.
The stakes are high for AEO keyword gaps in this new search era . When a buyer asks an answer engine to recommend a product or solution, rather than a page of links to choose from, they get a paraphrased response or a shortlist directly from AI.
The evidence is in the data: HubSpot’s own research of 3,063 CRM software purchase decision-makers found that 42% of CRM software buyers now use AI search as part of their evaluation, and it’s the strongest predictor of purchase intent HubSpot tracks. Referral traffic from AI tools like ChatGPT and Gemini has also tripled over the past year, according to Search Engine Land . If a brand isn’t showing up in the prompts that map to its category, it’s being left off the shortlist before a buyer ever visits a website.
The following bar chart from the Search Engine Land article shows the aggregate referral traffic by month in 2025. Monthly volume climbed steadily throughout the year, with December’s referral traffic roughly three times higher than January’s. The rising traffic reinforces the importance of the AEO keyword gap. More people are searching using AI tools.
Important note: An SEO keyword gap and an AEO keywords gap don’t tell the same story, and closing one doesn’t close the other. A page can rank on page one of Google for a term and still never get pulled into an AI-generated answer for that same topic. BrightEdge’s analysis of AI Overviews (AIO) found that only about 17% of sources cited in AIOs also rank in the organic top 10, meaning roughly five out of six AIO citations pull from content that never appears on page one of traditional results.
Pro tip: While an SEO keyword gap shows where content is missing from rankings, it can’t show where content is ranking well and still getting skipped over in AI-generated answers.
A traditional keyword gap report answers one question: Which terms does a competitor rank for that a brand doesn’t?
Gaps between AEO versus SEO are not the same thing. The comparison needs more dimensions than that, because answer engines aren’t just matching keywords. AEO keyword research prioritizes questions, entities, answer formats, and citation potential.
Auditing an AEO keyword gap is the first step to improving visibility and staying competitive in search. There are four essential steps that make up an AEO keywords gap audit:
Google Search Console (GSC) shows which queries are already driving impressions and clicks to a website. While GSC is largely an SEO tool with keyword research capabilities and AEO features in beta, the data is still transferable to AEO (also known as GEO ). Queries that are already gaining impressions and clicks are, in theory, associated with your website; the brand already has authority there, which may transfer to AIO.
Start by exporting data and reviewing keywords in Google Sheets or in an Excel spreadsheet. Look for:
Export data from GSC by visiting the Performance report, altering the data range, then clicking Export.
The following screenshot shows a Google Sheet I exported that contains all queries for my brand in Google Search Console. I used a formula to calculate how many words were in 1,000 queries, then sorted by the biggest value.
=IF(TRIM(B1)=””, 0, LEN(TRIM(B1)) - LEN(SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(B1), “ “, “”)) + 1)
The queries highlighted in green are most interesting to me.
I can see B2B software companies struggling to tie pipeline to won deals, which is a common challenge I can solve! From this information, I could create pages and content to support this audience with a call to action to get in touch.
Before creating content, it helps to look at the search engine results pages (SERPs). Even a manual review provides insights into patterns. Next, pull up the SERP for a target query and note:
Once I’ve established what’s being prioritized in SERPs, I’d create a similar page to maximize visibility.
Sales calls, support tickets, and community forums are full of the exact phrasing customers use when they’re trying to solve a problem, which is often closer to how someone would prompt an answer engine.
Pulling recurring questions from these sources and checking whether current content answers them directly is a fast way to surface gaps that neither a keyword tool nor a competitor audit would catch on their own. Start by reviewing:
Here’s an example of a question on HubSpot’s Community , likely the kind of question that gets asked in AI search all the time:
This question relates to speed differences between WordPress and HubSpot. HubSpot has a comparison between WordPress and HubSpot . This mini content gap analysis demonstrates that HubSpot could edit the comparison to include information about page speed to satisfy queries like this. This mini content gap analysis reveals which content edits or new pieces will improve performance in search generative experiences.
A company’s top competitors in AI answer engine search are often different than the ones showing up in a traditional SERP. To expose where the real competition is, run a set of prompts related to a brand’s category and note:
Which formats those citations favor (comparison pages, listicles, product pages) Start by running category-level prompts through ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overview that a prospective customer might type before they’ve decided on a vendor. Log the response, the domains cited, and the page type behind each citation in a spreadsheet.
Here’s an example: Running a prompt like “best CRM for small sales teams” surfaced listicle-style blog posts and Reddit posts as citations. The domains were not any vendor’s own website. The pages cited most consistently were structured as head-to-head comparisons with pricing tables, reviews, pros and cons, and more.
From this, marketers know what they need to do to improve brand visibility in these searches. Marketing needs to work on connections with third-party websites or PR, since this search is dominated by them.
Once the foundational research is done, it’s time to optimize websites with a view of closing AEO gaps. Start with an inventory of existing pages mapped against the core topics a brand should own.
Does each page directly answer identified, specific questions? Or does it talk around a topic without committing to a clear answer? A page can cover a topic thoroughly and still fail this test if it never states a direct answer an engine could lift and cite. Sticking with the examples above, a content review for each insight might be:
Run together, these AEO keywords gap audit steps replace guesswork with a documented view of where a brand is answering clearly, where it’s talking around a topic without committing to an answer, and where competitors are winning the citation instead.
With all the information and data from the first three steps, marketers have a much easier time getting buy-in from teams to create or edit content, or even securing budget from stakeholders to get the work done.
Not every gap surfaced by the four steps above is worth closing. Some questions get asked but sit outside what the business actually sells or wants to specialize in.
For example, in my Google Search Console export, I found many queries related to ecommerce websites or sites with thousands of SKUs. While I could create content to help these brands and increase my visibility in AI tools, I don’t target ecommerce brands. Since they’re not my ideal client profile (ICP), I needn’t try to get in front of them.
Sort queries and actions by how much they help your brand and, importantly, revenue. Think about:
Once the list is sorted, it helps to have a baseline read on where the brand already stands compared to competitors.
HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is a free tool that scores how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity characterize a brand across five dimensions: Sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position. Based on those scores, AI Search Grader generates a free optimization report companies can use as a baseline to benchmark how AI represents competitors.
Once a gap is confirmed and prioritized, the job shifts from research to writing something an answer engine can actually lift. Answer-ready content uses direct answers, supporting evidence, and consistent entity naming in a specific structure that makes it easier for AI answer engines to extract as standalone citations.
If a question appears as a heading within a page, the first sentence or two after the heading should answer the question completely, in language close to how it was asked. Then, include any nuance, caveats, or supporting details.
Front-loading a direct answer fixes the “talks around it” pages that get flagged during the content review. A page might already cover the question somewhere in the copy, but if the answer isn’t stated plainly near a heading that matches the question, an answer engine has nothing clean to cite.
Once the core question is answered, build out the related questions a buyer would ask next. Each supporting question gets its own heading and direct answer, turning one page into coverage for a cluster of related prompts.
Link to pages that support the claim, such as a case study, a product spec, or a data page. Link in from related content covering the same topic cluster.
Technically, marketers can perform all the AEO keyword gap research steps we’ve outlined manually. But it’s incredibly tedious, inaccurate, and reductive. Manual AEO keyword research is generally a mistake because it is inefficient and captures only a single snapshot in time.
HubSpot AEO helps marketers track brand visibility, competitor presence, and citation gaps across answer engines. It extends visibility tracking beyond traditional search to answer engines like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, turning that manual audit into an ongoing trend report rather than a one-off exercise redone from scratch every quarter.
Manual monitoring only captures a single point in time: Whatever a prompt returns on the day it’s checked, until someone remembers to check again. HubSpot AEO runs that tracking continuously, sending each tracked prompt to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity every day and aggregating the responses into a Brand Visibility score, the percentage of answers where the brand is mentioned.
The benefit? Visibility becomes a trend . No brand can expect to show up in every search every time, but if visibility is trending in the right direction, it’s positive. Marketers can see a score move week over week, catch a dip as it happens, and see it broken down by engine, rather than waiting for a quarterly recheck to notice something changed.
Instead of manually running a handful of prompts and noting which competitor names came back, HubSpot AEO runs that comparison continuously and structures the results: Which competitors are named, how consistently, and whether that shifts over time.
The tool tracks Share of Voice, showing marketers the percentage of citations across tracked prompts that mention their brand versus named competitors.
Keeping track of which domains get cited and why, especially across multiple prompts, is complex and time-consuming. HubSpot AEO provides comprehensive citation analysis that shows which domains, content types, and channels influence AI-generated answers. Marketers get competitive insights on what’s actually shaping the answers in their category.
Once gaps are visible, HubSpot AEO can suggest how to close them based on its competitive analysis, effectively automating a slice of the prioritization work: Which gaps are answerable, which are most relevant, and which are at a funnel stage worth prioritizing
HubSpot AEO doesn’t replace human judgment; a tool can’t know a brand’s ICP the way a marketer does. But it narrows the list down to an efficient, informed working set teams can build on.
Acting on findings is where Marketing Hub’s SEO software comes in. AEO in Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise uses CRM data to suggest relevant prompts to track, so the prompts a brand monitors reflect its own audience and offerings. From there, Marketing Hub helps teams turn AEO recommendations into published content, surface prioritized SEO fixes, find topics worth building out, and connect Google Search Console to see impressions and click-through rate as new content goes live.
The real value of tracking an AEO keywords gap comes from watching the numbers move over weeks, months, year-over-year, and seasonally.
Visibility trending upward across tracked prompts indicates that recent content and citation-building efforts are working. A flat or declining trend, even with new content published, is a signal that something in the approach needs to change, whether it’s the prompts being tracked, the content format, or the citation sources being pursued.
Citations tell a more specific story than visibility alone. A rising visibility score paired with flat or declining citations suggests a brand is being mentioned in AI-generated answers but not cited as a source, which points to a perception problem rather than a content gap. Watching which domains and content types earn citations over time shows whether content efforts are actually being recognized as authoritative or whether competitors and third-party sites are still doing the influencing.
Prompt coverage matters just as much as any single score. Buyer language shifts, new competitors enter a category, and the questions people ask answer engines change accordingly. Reviewing and expanding the tracked prompt set on a regular cadence keeps the overall measurement effort aligned with what buyers are currently asking.
Visibility, citations, and prompt coverage have no strategic value unless they generate measurable leads, deals, or revenue attributed to AI-referred traffic.
Assisted business impact, leads, deals, and revenue that can be traced back to AI-referred traffic or citation-driven visibility turn AEO from a trend line into results worth reporting to leadership. Visibility and citations are leading indicators; pipeline and revenue are the metrics that justify continued investment.
Pro tip: Benchmark against the industry, too. A visibility score that’s flat for two months could reflect a stalled strategy or an industry-wide shift in how a given answer engine cites sources across the board. Comparing brand-level trends against industry-level data is the only way to tell the difference.
AI Search Sensor is a free, beta dashboard that tracks volatility in how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity cite brands and surface content, along with industry-level visibility benchmarks. Paired with a team’s own AEO data, it adds context for judging whether a shift in their numbers reflects a market-wide movement or a problem with their own strategy, before they react to the wrong one.
Outside of a full audit, running a handful of category-relevant prompts through ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity manually and noting whether a brand or its competitors are cited helps confirm whether a gap likely exists before committing time to a deeper analysis.
SEO keyword research prioritizes search volume and ranking difficulty for specific terms. AEO keyword research shifts the focus to the prompts, questions, entities, and answer formats behind those terms, since that’s what determines whether content gets cited rather than just ranked.
Pages that answer one specific question directly, with supporting evidence and consistent entity naming, tend to perform best, especially comparison pages, definitional content, and FAQ-style pages. Vague or broadly scoped pages rarely get cited even when they technically cover the topic.
Revisiting AEO keywords gap quarterly is a reasonable baseline for most teams, though categories with fast-moving competitors or frequent buyer-language shifts may warrant a monthly check. The prompt set and citation landscape both change faster than a typical SEO keyword list does.
Yes. Visibility, citation, and share-of-voice metrics are independent of traditional search rankings, since they measure whether and how often a brand appears in AI-generated answers rather than where a page appears on a search results page.
Buyers are already asking answer engines to make shortlists for them, and every unanswered prompt is a chance for a competitor to be the name that comes back instead.
Closing an AEO keywords gap means running a repeatable audit, prioritizing by business relevance and answerability, rebuilding content so it leads with a direct answer, and tracking visibility and citations over time rather than treating any of this as a one-time project.
I’ve seen what’s on the other side of getting this right. Clients of mine are sending out six-figure proposals sourced from leads that began with a prompt in Gemini or another AI tool, rather than a Google search.
HubSpot AEO is built for exactly this shift: Tracking visibility, comparing against competitors, and surfacing citation gaps continuously, so closing an AEO keywords gap becomes a measurable KPI and a marketing target.

title: How do I benchmark my AI search performance against my industry?
content:
Measuring success is a leading challenge for answer engine optimization (AEO) that marketers report today. In HubSpot’s State of AEO 2026 report, it was the top challenge among B2B marketers at 23%; among B2C marketers, 26% cited it, behind only understanding how AEO works at 29%.
Traditional search metrics still matter, but they answer different questions. Clicks and impressions in Google Search Console, and even website visits, don’t show whether answer engines mention or cite a brand, or how often that happens compared with competitors.
This guide lays out a repeatable process for benchmarking AEO using citation rate, share of voice, platform-level normalization, and executive-ready reporting. Together, those measures turn one-off prompt checks into a benchmark marketing teams can track and explain to leadership.
Ranking well in traditional search means a page appears on a search engine results page (SERP). A user can then click a result to visit the source.
HubSpot distinguishes AEO mentions from citations this way: A mention names a brand in an AI-generated answer without a linked source, while a citation is an attributed source reference or linked URL. For this guide, a brand-level citation means an attributed source or linked URL from the brand’s domain.
Answer engine optimization measures a different layer of search visibility: whether and how a brand or its content appears inside synthesized answers. AI-generated search features can also change click behavior. Ahrefs found that the presence of a Google AI Overview correlated with a 58% lower average click-through rate for the top-ranking page in its December 2025 data.
Traditional SEO metrics measure how pages perform in search results. AEO metrics measure whether brands and sources appear inside AI-generated answers.
Featured resource: AI and SEO: What AI means for the future of SEO [Expert Tips & Interview] .
The following table shows common SEO metrics alongside AEO benchmarks. I cover the AEO benchmarks in more detail in the next section.
AEO benchmarking measures how often a brand appears or is cited across answer engines relative to a defined competitor set. Because generated answers can vary from run to run, these measures are estimates based on a defined set of prompts, platform, and collection window, not fixed rankings.
For Google AI Overviews specifically, BrightEdge’s analysis found that about 17% of cited sources also ranked in the organic top 10, meaning roughly five out of six citations came from outside page 1. BrightEdge reported 24% top-10 overlap in healthcare and 11% in finance. That does not make organic rankings irrelevant; it shows that organic ranking and AI Overview citation overlap can differ substantially by industry, so teams should measure both.
The four benchmarks below help measure and organize visibility in answer engines. They do not measure website or revenue impact on their own, so use them alongside traffic, conversion, and pipeline measures rather than treating them as replacements.
In an experiment involving more than 500 queries across 20 platforms , Robert Carnes found that AI chatbots performed better on some direct-action prompts and could build arguments for opinion-based queries. At the same time, traditional search remained useful for specific and local information. The mixed result matters for benchmarking: Some AI interactions can satisfy a query without a click, but traditional search still plays an important role.
Separately, HubSpot’s State of AEO 2026 report says 44% of surveyed marketers have made a business purchase based on brands they discovered through answer engines.
In a separate survey of more than 200 B2B decision-makers, 42% said an AI recommendation made a brand seem “more trustworthy — if AI recommends it, it’s probably vetted.” The research on B2B decision-makers and AI search found only 11% said an AI recommendation made a brand seem less trustworthy.
As Amanda Sellers, a former SEO and AEO strategist at HubSpot, puts it in the State of AEO report, “Answer engines can achieve a level of personalization not possible with traditional search, which aids in the consideration process along a path to purchase. By the time these buyers land on a web page, they are much more qualified.”
The takeaway is not that AEO replaces SEO. It is that brand discovery and evaluation can happen before a website click, so marketers need visibility measures for answer engines alongside traditional SEO metrics.
Citation rate indicates how often a brand or domain is explicitly cited in answer-engine responses within a defined set of prompts.
Citation rate = (Number of prompts where the brand or domain is cited ÷ Total number of prompts) × 100
Use the citation rate as a baseline to determine whether attributable visibility is increasing or decreasing. Read it alongside share of voice, so you don’t interpret a percentage without competitive context.
Share of voice compares a brand’s mentions with named competitors across the same prompt set.
Share of voice = (Brand mentions ÷ Total mentions for the brand and tracked competitors) × 100
A 20% share of voice, compared with 8% for the next tracked competitor, indicates stronger relative visibility within the defined competitor set. It does not establish category leadership beyond the brands and prompts included in the benchmark.
For this benchmark, platform-level visibility means calculating citation rate and share of voice separately for each answer engine, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.
Platform-level visibility = Citation rate or share of voice calculated for one answer engine at a time
This prevents a blended average from hiding meaningful differences between platforms. A brand could have strong visibility in Perplexity and weak visibility in ChatGPT even when the overall average looks stable.
For this benchmark, query-set segmentation means grouping tracked prompts into useful categories, such as topic, buyer stage, use case, or product line, and calculating the citation rate or share of voice within each group.
Segment-level visibility = Citation rate or share of voice calculated for one defined prompt segment
Segmentation helps expose gaps that an aggregate rate can hide. A brand might have healthy overall visibility while rarely appearing in high-intent comparison prompts.
HubSpot AEO can automate prompt tracking, brand visibility, competitor share of voice, citation analysis, sentiment, and prioritized recommendations across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. In Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise, CRM data powers more specific recommendations. Standalone HubSpot AEO starts at $50 per month, or $45 per month when billed annually. It is also included with Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise.
Featured Resource: AI SEO: How to use AI to improve your SEO workflow
Industry benchmarks are useful only when you compare like with like. Compare a brand’s citation rate using the same metric across a consistent prompt set, competitor set, answer engine, and collection window.
AI Search Sensor provides industry-level context for answer-engine visibility trends. The free public dashboard tracks estimated visibility, citation share, AI-referred traffic, citation patterns, and answer-engine volatility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.
Do not compare a brand’s citation rate directly with AI Search Sensor’s visibility score or citation share as though those metrics were interchangeable. Use the industry data as category context, then evaluate the brand with consistent brand-level metrics.
Here’s a look at visibility scores across the marketing industry:
AI Search Sensor is a free public dashboard currently in beta. It tracks industry-level and market-wide patterns across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity rather than reporting a specific brand’s own performance. Marketers can use it in four ways.
Tip: AI Search Sensor does not report a brand’s own visibility or citation share. For brand-specific prompt tracking and competitor comparison, HubSpot AEO adds that layer.
For brand-specific benchmarking, HubSpot AEO includes:
Industry data provides context; brand-specific data shows what is happening to the individual brand. HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is a free, one-time check that provides a snapshot across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, including visibility, sentiment, and competitive positioning. Here’s how AI Search Grader looks:
AI Search Grader is useful as a one-time baseline, but an ongoing benchmark needs a defined query set, competitor set, and rerun cadence.
A query set is the list of prompts used to calculate citation rate, share of voice, and related benchmarks. It should reflect questions buyers actually ask in the category, not just the brand’s preferred keywords. A useful starting set should cover several types of prompts:
If you are testing manually, start with a set small enough to rerun consistently and treat the result as directional. For a more comprehensive audit, Discovered Labs’ AEO benchmarking guide recommends mapping 50–200 high-intent questions and notes that statistical confidence can require hundreds of query variations across multiple platforms and repeated tests.
Next, build a fixed competitor set. Run the query set first and record the brands that recur in mentions and citations. Then choose a named group that includes direct competitors and other AI-visible peers that buyers are genuinely likely to compare.
Keep the query and competitor sets stable within a reporting cycle. When a material product, market, or competitor change requires an update, version the benchmark and record what changed so earlier results remain interpretable. Label Studio’s guide to evolving AI benchmarks explains that standardized task sets make results comparable across runs and that benchmark strategies should evolve as systems mature.
Track the benchmark weekly to notice trends. Review the query and competitor lists quarterly, or sooner after a material category, product, or competitive change, rather than rewriting them between every benchmark run.
Pro tip: Manual tracking can work for an initial benchmark. As the number of prompts, platforms, and repeated runs grows, automation reduces the burden of collection and logging. HubSpot AEO is one option for ongoing prompt, competitor, visibility, and citation tracking.
Raw citation counts from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity are not directly comparable on their own. Normalize the testing process first, then report each platform separately. Account for two kinds of variation.
Do not solve that variation by combining all platforms into a single blended number. Calculate citation rate and share of voice separately for each engine. For example, a 30% citation rate on Perplexity and an 8% citation rate on ChatGPT are two platform-level results, not inputs to be averaged.
To compare large language models (LLMs) fairly for AEO benchmarking, use the same fixed prompt list, the same market or location settings where possible, a consistent collection window, and repeated runs when resources allow. Discovered Labs’ AEO benchmarking guidance notes that one-off manual checks are vulnerable to answer variability and personalization. A stable testing set and a documented benchmark version make changes over time easier to interpret.
A benchmark becomes useful when it changes what the team does next. Once you’ve established citation rate, share of voice, platform-level visibility, and query-set segmentation, move from measurement to prioritization.
Start with the prompt segments where the brand is weakest. For each missed prompt, inspect the URLs, domains, source channels, and content types the answer engine actually cites. Use those observed patterns rather than assuming that a particular prompt type will always favor a particular format. Classify each priority gap.
Prioritize gaps based on business relevance and repeatability, rather than trying to fix every missed prompt at once.
For more guidance on creating source-worthy content, see How to Write Content that Generative AI Search Engines Will Cite, According to Experts . For additional ideas on adapting content strategy as search changes, see 6 Steps Bloggers are Taking to Prepare for AI in Search [New Data] .
HubSpot AEO supports this ongoing stage by tracking brand visibility, competitors, citations, and prompts over time and turning those patterns into prioritized recommendations.
An executive-ready benchmark report should summarize the decisions the data supports, not reproduce every prompt and platform result. Include:
Leadership usually does not need the full prompt log. Keep that working-level detail with the marketing, SEO, or AEO team.
Marketing and SEO should own the query set, competitor set, citation analysis, and content response. Bring revenue operations (RevOps) into the reporting process as the team begins connecting AI-referred traffic and other marketing activity to CRM definitions, pipeline, and revenue reporting.
HubSpot AEO tracks prompts, brand visibility, competitors, citations, and recommendations. When AEO is used inside Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise, CRM data also powers more specific recommendations. Marketing analytics and dashboards can report on website, campaign, CRM, and revenue outcomes, and teams can pair those results with AEO visibility metrics, using the AEO dashboard or HubSpot’s beta AEO API, so leadership sees business results next to visibility.
For a team without a brand-specific benchmark, AI Search Sensor offers a free starting point for industry context. It tracks broad AI visibility, citation, traffic, and volatility trends across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. It does not show the individual brand’s own visibility or pipeline impact, so treat it as category context rather than a substitute for brand-level measurement.
For an active benchmarking program, rerun the benchmark weekly to notice trends. Review the query set and competitor list quarterly, or sooner after a material product, category, or competitive change. When the set changes, document the new version so you don’t treat pre- and post-change results as perfectly comparable.
Marketing and SEO should usually own the day-to-day benchmark because they define the prompts, track visibility and citations, and turn gaps into content or distribution work. A dedicated AEO team can own the process where one exists. Bring revenue operations into the reporting layer when AI-referred traffic, CRM data, pipeline, or revenue become part of the benchmark story.
Spot-check a sample of detected citations by running the same prompts manually and confirming that the reported brand mention or linked source appears. Match the answer engine, prompt, and testing conditions as closely as possible. Because generated answers can vary between runs, an occasional difference between a tool’s recorded result and a later manual check does not automatically mean the tool was wrong.
A small, infrequent benchmark can stay manual as long as the team can rerun it consistently and keep a clean record of the results. Automation becomes more useful when repeated runs across multiple engines, larger prompt sets, competitor tracking, and result logging start consuming enough time that the team cannot maintain a consistent benchmark manually.
A useful AI search benchmark turns “we seem to show up sometimes” into a repeatable measurement program. Keep the query and competitor sets consistent, separate results by answer engine, track citation rate and share of voice over time, use industry data as context, and report visibility alongside traffic and pipeline outcomes.
AEO does not replace traditional SEO measurement. The two answer different questions, and teams need both to understand how brands are discovered across search results and AI-generated answers.
For teams ready to automate ongoing brand-level measurement, HubSpot AEO tracks visibility, prompts, competitors, citations, and prioritized recommendations across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.
